excerpt: The Road to Talofofo tells the poignant story of Kimiko Nishikawa—a ten-year-old girl orphaned in the darkness of WWII Guam—and the unexpected sanctuary that carried her from tragedy into a lifetime of quiet faith as Sister Antonieta. Clean, honest, and deeply moving, it is a story of how love survives the worst of human conflict.
shortText:
It was not a fancy dinner, but it was one no one would forget. Outside, the war was waiting; inside, a family was sitting down together for the last time.

Kimiko Nishikawa was ten, and though her Japanese was shaky, she knew enough to feel the cold shift in the room. Her father spoke to them with tears in his eyes. He told them to hold tight to each other, to treat their neighbors kindly, and never to grow lazy. Then he poured the wine in a small, solemn ritual. Kimiko looked around the table at the wet cheeks and tight faces, every one of them braced for what was coming next.

They ate quickly. There was no time to linger. They packed what they could carry and agreed to split up, aiming to meet again down the road in Talofofo.

Years later, as Sister Antonieta, Kimiko remembered how her father had laid out their roles that night. Taiichi, the eldest, took the family cash and important papers. Michiko, Nagako, and Hiroji were set in charge of the food. Splitting the family was a risk, but keeping everyone together felt like a bigger one.

Michiko, Hiroji, and Nagako set off first for Talofofo. They slipped away as planned, but the family never saw them again.

A little while later, Kimiko set out with her parents, her brother Taiichi, and little Noboru. They made their way to a crowded cave where dozens of others were huddled, waiting out the darkness in low, worried whispers. Before long, the silence split wide open—a bomb landed, sending sharp debris through the air. Kimiko was hurt, but she stayed quiet and survived.

In the days that followed, her father showed a quiet, practical kind of grace. Under cover of night, Mr. Nishikawa and Taiichi would crawl out into the dark to catch rainwater and gather what they could from nearby sugarcane fields.

One night, the cane rustled a little too loudly. A sudden crack of gunfire cut through the dark. Mr. Nishikawa fell, mortally wounded. Taiichi carried his father’s body back into the cave, and with that heavy burden, the old life came to a end.

With her husband gone, Mrs. Nishikawa knew they couldn't stay. She gathered her children and tried to lead them back toward home under the dark sky. But as they picked their way through the tall stalks, shots rang out once more, and she too was killed.

Kimiko thought she was completely alone in the world. But in the middle of that wreck of a day, Alcalde Ada found her. He took her in, fed her, and gave her a place to rest when everything else was falling apart.

When the war finally cleared, Kimiko took a new name—Antonieta Ada—and in time, took her vows. She spent the rest of her days in the quiet routine of the convent, where the old sharp memories slowly gave way to peace. Looking back on it all, Sister Tonie saw a quiet, steady thread running through the worst of it—a grace that brought her to a home when she needed one most, and held her fast until the end.
author: Lexi Zotomayor
